title: Retinotopic reconnection of retinal ganglion cell axons to brain targets

concept.text: The proposed innovation would restore the biological connection between the retina and the brain after optic-nerve damage. Retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) carry visual information through their long nerve fibers, called axons. The goal is to make axons grow through the damaged pathway, reach appropriate visual centers in the brain, and form functional connections that support useful form vision. This extends the retinal-regeneration goal described by the National Eye Institute’s Audacious Goals Initiative: replacing damaged retinal cells and restoring their connections to brain visual centers.

Retinotopic reconnection means preserving an appropriate spatial relationship between locations in the retina and the brain’s representation of the visual scene. Simply getting some axons into the brain would not establish this capability. The intended outcome is organized transmission that lets a person distinguish spatial patterns and forms. Relevant targets include the lateral geniculate nucleus and superior colliculus, but the supplied evidence does not establish successful mature-human reconnection across this complete target scope.

Two biological starting points must be distinguished. Surviving mature RGCs might regrow their damaged axons; where RGCs have died, replacement cells may also be necessary. Replacement RGCs would need to integrate with retinal circuits as well as send axons toward the brain. Advanced glaucoma can therefore require both cell replacement and pathway reconstruction, rather than axon growth alone.

significance.text: Optic-nerve damage can interrupt the delivery of retinal visual information even when other parts of the eye retain useful function. Current glaucoma treatment primarily seeks to lower pressure and prevent additional damage; preserving an eye or keeping transplanted tissue alive does not itself reconstruct lost central connections. Restoring useful form vision through new RGC-to-brain connections would establish a major new capability: biological repair of the damaged visual pathway in the population successfully treated.

Potential applications include glaucoma, ischemic and hereditary optic neuropathies, and optic-nerve trauma. These are candidate applications, not an established common indication. Their differences in cell survival, injury location, disease activity, and remaining visual circuitry mean that success in one condition would require additional evidence before being generalized to another. Even successful reconnection would not establish that every form or severity of optic neuropathy had become repairable.

A conditional downstream possibility is that principles learned about adult axon growth, guidance, and functional targeting could inform repair elsewhere in the central nervous system. Applying them to spinal-cord injury would require a further breakthrough; optic-nerve reconnection would not by itself demonstrate repair of other neural pathways. Likewise, repairing the eye-to-brain connection would address only one component of vision restoration when photoreceptors, retinal support tissue, or other visual structures are also damaged.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability in this record is coordinated long-distance growth and spatially accurate functional reconnection of human RGC axons. Limited adult regenerative capacity is only one obstacle. Growing axons must also negotiate damaged tissue, inhibitory scarring, and the structures of the optic-nerve head. The reviewed material identifies the lamina cribrosa, a set of perforated fibroelastic plates through which RGC axons pass, as a significant barrier to regrowth and guidance. These findings support impaired adult regeneration without requiring the categorical claim that all growth programs shut down after development.

Growth must be coupled to correct destination selection and functional synapse formation. Axons reaching a central visual nucleus would still need to establish sufficiently organized connections to transmit spatial information. The reviewed material identifies uncertainty about retinotopic connections to the lateral geniculate nucleus; it does not establish that extending axons alone will restore the mapping needed for useful form vision. Reaching the optic-nerve head is therefore an intermediate achievement, not completion of the pathway.

Where the original RGCs have been lost, an additional barrier is supplying suitable replacement neurons and integrating them at both ends of the pathway. NEI describes humans as having little capacity to replace these retinal neurons naturally. A complete strategy for advanced cell loss would consequently need to address replacement-cell survival and retinal integration alongside axon guidance and central connectivity.

current_state.text: NEI’s Audacious Goals Initiative identifies photoreceptors and RGCs as regeneration targets and explicitly includes restoration of connections to brain visual centers. Its 23 October 2023 article described a roadmap of milestones to reach before clinical trials of regenerative retinal therapies. The roadmap covered safety, patient selection, efficacy endpoints, clinical controls, regulatory considerations, and commercial viability. This establishes a dated translational planning effort, rather than a demonstrated clinical cure or a comprehensive account of subsequent progress.

Lu and colleagues, published in Nature on 2 December 2020, reported that OSK reprogramming promoted axon regeneration after injury and improved vision in mouse glaucoma and ageing models. The supplied review supports these findings through the article’s subscription preview and associated materials. They are mouse results and do not establish retinotopic reconnection or restoration of human form vision.

The quantitative statement that treatment recovered about half of the lost visual acuity comes from the authors’ peer-review responses concerning an optomotor response assay. It should be understood as their characterization of that mouse result, not as an independently rechecked numerical analysis of the primary data. The authors explicitly distinguished the visual improvement from restoration of eyesight after optic-nerve crush. Their supplementary discussion also described the microbead glaucoma model as more acute than chronic, limiting its equivalence to chronic human glaucoma.

Access to the 2020 study was incomplete for evaluating its full experimental evidence. The supplied review had a subscription preview, a complete supplementary-information file, a largely textless additional PDF, and a peer-review file truncated on page 49. The inspected captions and extracted prose do not substitute for examination of all figures, methods, or numerical data. These limitations bound what can be concluded from the supplied materials; they do not show that the reported mouse findings are false.

Cavaleri and colleagues’ Brain Sciences review, published on 30 October 2025, reported that the first human whole-eye transplant maintained viable donor tissue at one year without restoring functional vision. This is evidence that tissue viability and visual-pathway restoration are distinct outcomes. The account is secondary evidence rather than the original clinical report. Although the retained text is truncated in its references, the supplied review includes the relevant transplant outcome and discussion of retinotopic targeting barriers.

The earlier research attributed to a 29 April 2026 Science Translational Medicine report the claims that human stem-cell-derived RGCs could reach the optic-nerve head and respond to light in rodents, while central synaptic integration remained difficult. No document or abstract for that citation was retained in the supplied evidence. Its date, authorship, experimental scope, and findings therefore remain unverified here. These claims remain possible partial advances, but cannot be presented as established achievements on this record.

The supplied dated evidence supports substantial remaining barriers to human functional reconnection. It does not establish the field’s status comprehensively as of 1 November 2026 because no freshness-search record was supplied. The innovation is therefore a target capability in this record, with encouraging preclinical findings and an unresolved current worldwide clinical status.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: enroll people with clearly documented optic-nerve discontinuity or advanced glaucomatous axon loss, and show that treatment creates new axonal connections reaching appropriate central visual nuclei. Converging anatomical and physiological evidence should support that interpretation. Where RGCs have died, the demonstration should account for any replacement cells required. These are proposed criteria for this concept, not established clinical or regulatory standards.
completion_criteria.label: New axonal connections reach appropriate central visual nuclei in people

completion_criteria.text: Proposed functional evidence should include reproducible light-evoked cortical responses together with a prespecified, useful improvement in visual field or acuity beyond matched untreated controls. Spatially resolved testing should establish appropriate eye-to-brain mapping and performance on form-vision tasks. Cortical responses alone would not demonstrate useful vision, and improved vision alone would not establish that newly grown connections caused the benefit.
completion_criteria.label: Useful mapped form-vision gains exceed controls with reproducible cortical responses

completion_criteria.text: Proposed causal testing should distinguish new reconnection from recovery or improved use of surviving pathways, particularly in glaucoma, where some axons may remain functional. Eye survival, light responses confined to the retina, or axons stopping at the optic-nerve head would not meet the intended endpoint. This distinction is essential to demonstrating the specific biological repair claimed by the title.
completion_criteria.label: Causal testing distinguishes new reconnection from surviving pathway recovery

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries should include repeatable results across participants, confirmation by independent investigators, and follow-up sufficient to assess persistence of useful vision and treatment safety. Studies should specify the diseases, injury severities, residual circuitry, and cell-replacement requirements under which benefit occurs. Finite demonstrations would establish that tested breadth, not universal repairability. Human pathfinding feasibility, suitable efficacy thresholds, and the time required to achieve durable reconnection remain uncertain. NEI’s roadmap supports addressing endpoints, controls, safety, and patient selection, without endorsing these exact proposed tests.
completion_criteria.label: Report independent replication, persistence and safety follow-up, and tested benefit boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: OPH-02, Biological reconstruction of foveal cones, RPE, and their blood supply, addresses the image-sensing and supporting tissues upstream of RGC output. OPH-01 addresses transmission from RGCs to the brain. An eye with damage at both levels could require both capabilities. Replacement RGCs fall within the reconnection problem here and should not be confused with photoreceptor or RPE replacement.

Roster-based synthesis: OPH-10, Arrest of glaucomatous ganglion-cell death when pressure is not the lever, concerns preservation of threatened RGCs. OPH-01 concerns restoring connections after axonal damage or cell loss. Protection could preserve the substrate needed for regeneration or prevent further loss after repair, but arresting cell death would not itself demonstrate new central connections.

Roster-based synthesis: OPH-05, Patterned vision from the brain when the eye cannot send signals, shares the functional goal of visual perception but approaches it through brain-based stimulation rather than reconstruction of the biological RGC pathway. OPH-09, Reopening of the human visual critical period, concerns visual-system plasticity; it could potentially help the brain interpret restored input, but would not itself demonstrate axon growth or accurate targeting.

Roster-based synthesis: OPH-07, One programmable repair for many photoreceptor and RPE gene defects, OPH-08, Reperfusion of established retinal capillary dropout, and OPH-11, Prevention of progression from early or intermediate AMD to late AMD, address distinct genetic, vascular, and degenerative retinal problems. Their preservation or repair of retinal function could complement OPH-01 in a multiply damaged eye, but none substitutes for restoring a disrupted RGC-to-brain connection.

Roster-based synthesis: OPH-03, Reversal of established cataract without removing the lens, and OPH-04, A manufactured cornea that clears vascularized stromal opacity, address optical transmission before light reaches the retina. OPH-06, A closed-loop control that sets axial eye growth, addresses regulation of eye dimensions. These remain separate innovations: optical clarity and suitable eye geometry can matter for usable vision, but do not establish neural reconnection.

unresolved_issues: The 2026 Science Translational Medicine citation lacks a retained artifact; its identity, publication date, authorship, experimental results, and central-connectivity limitations remain unverified.
No freshness-search record was supplied, so the dated evidence cannot establish the worldwide clinical status of human retinotopic reconnection as of 1 November 2026.

The approximately half-acuity recovery figure is an author characterization from peer-review responses; primary numerical data and complete methods were not independently assessed in the supplied review.
The Zhang citation’s retained redirect text does not permit assessment of the attributed quotation or article contents.

Suitable clinical efficacy thresholds, durability requirements, safety boundaries, disease-specific applicability, and the development timeline have not been established by the supplied materials.

brief.title: Restoring sight by reconnecting the eye to the brain
possible: People who lose sight after optic-nerve damage could regain the ability to distinguish shapes and spatial patterns. Nerve fibers would regrow from the retina, the eye’s light-sensitive tissue, to the brain. Their connections would preserve the layout of the visual scene, so signals from different places in the eye reach the right places in the brain.
why: For people with glaucoma, treatment mainly aims to prevent further damage. Rebuilding the eye-to-brain connection would offer a way to recover lost vision. It could also help people whose optic nerves were damaged by injury, interrupted blood supply or inherited disease.

sources.showed: The institute established a research programme aimed at replacing damaged retinal cells and restoring their connections to the brain.
sources.cited_for: Restoring sight requires both retinal repair and connections to the brain.
sources.not_established: A research programme does not demonstrate restored eye-to-brain connections or useful vision in people.

sources.showed: Its projects study nerve-fiber growth, guidance toward brain targets, and the survival and integration of replacement retinal cells.
sources.cited_for: Replacing lost cells and connecting them within the eye and to the brain are distinct parts of restoring vision.
sources.not_established: These projects do not demonstrate replacement cells completing a functional visual pathway in people.

sources.showed: The authors developed a roadmap for moving retinal repair therapies toward human trials, covering safety, patient selection, measures of benefit and comparison groups.
sources.cited_for: Human trials need clear measures of benefit, suitable comparison groups and safety assessment.
sources.not_established: The roadmap does not demonstrate a treatment or establish the exact tests needed to prove mapped reconnection.

sources.showed: Changing gene activity in mouse retinal nerve cells promoted nerve-fiber regrowth after injury and improved vision in glaucoma and ageing models.
sources.quote: promotes axon regeneration after injury, and reverses vision loss in a mouse model of glaucoma and in aged mice.
sources.cited_for: Mouse experiments show that nerve-fiber regrowth and improvements in vision are biologically possible.
sources.not_established: The mouse results do not demonstrate correctly mapped reconnection or restored human form vision.

sources.who: Researchers studying stem-cell-derived retinal nerve cells
sources.showed: This is a rodent study of human stem-cell-derived retinal nerve cells and their growth and light responses.
sources.cited_for: The study concerns replacement retinal cells, a potential component of repairing the visual pathway.
sources.not_established: Growth toward the exit from the eye and retinal light responses would not establish functional connections to the brain.

sources.showed: Their review reported that a human whole-eye transplant kept donor tissue alive for a year without restoring functional vision. It also described barriers to guiding nerve fibers to brain targets.
sources.quote: While functional vision was not restored, the feasibility of such a transplant with viable tissue graft at one year was demonstrated.
sources.cited_for: Keeping eye tissue alive and restoring its visual connection to the brain are separate achievements.
sources.not_established: This review does not demonstrate that regrown human nerve fibers reach the right brain targets and restore useful vision.

shown: Lu and colleagues promoted nerve-fiber regrowth and improved vision in mice by changing gene activity in retinal nerve cells. Those results did not demonstrate the spatially organized reconnection needed here. Cavaleri and colleagues’ review reported living tissue after a human eye transplant, but no functional vision.
missing: Human retinal nerve fibers still need to grow through damaged tissue to the appropriate brain targets.
New connections must preserve spatial layout and transmit signals that support useful recognition of shapes.
Where retinal nerve cells have died, replacement cells must survive and connect within the retina as well as to the brain.

milestones.label: New nerve connections reach visual centers in people
milestones.explanation: Anatomical and electrical evidence would have to show new fibers reaching appropriate brain targets in people with documented pathway loss, accounting for replacement cells where needed. This would establish that growth completes the route.

milestones.label: Mapped vision improves beyond controls with repeatable brain responses
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to show repeatable brain responses to light and useful gains beyond untreated controls in visual sharpness or field, with correct spatial mapping and shape recognition. This would establish useful signal transmission.

milestones.label: New connections cause the improvement
milestones.explanation: Testing would have to distinguish benefits caused by new connections from recovery or better use of surviving pathways. This would establish that rebuilding the connection caused the improvement.

milestones.label: Independent studies confirm lasting, safe benefits and their limits
milestones.explanation: Results would have to repeat across participants and independent teams, with follow-up for lasting vision and safety and defined disease, damage and cell-replacement limits. This would establish where the treatment reliably helps.

uncertain: It remains unclear whether human nerve fibers can navigate the full route and form correctly organized connections at the required brain targets.
The size of a useful vision gain and the follow-up needed to establish lasting benefit and safety remain unsettled.
Success in one disease or degree of damage may not extend to others with different surviving cells and visual circuitry.

page.title: Retinotopic reconnection of retinal ganglion cells
page.definition: Human retinal ganglion cells, the retina’s output neurons, extend axons—their signal-carrying fibres—through a damaged optic nerve to brain visual targets. New connections preserve retinal spatial order, called retinotopy, and transmit signals that restore discrimination of spatial patterns.

goal.need: In 2020, glaucoma accounted for approximately 7.7 million adults aged 50 years or older with blindness or moderate-to-severe distance vision impairment worldwide, adding the two reported categories. Existing glaucoma treatments lower eye pressure to limit further damage but do not reverse vision already lost. Regenerating eye-to-brain connections addresses that loss.

figures.caption: Estimated glaucoma-related vision loss worldwide in adults aged 50 years or older, 2020
figures.note: Categories concern the better-seeing eye. Blindness means visual acuity below 3/60 or a central visual field below 10°. Moderate or severe impairment means acuity from 3/60 to below 6/18.

completion.title: New retinotopic retinal ganglion cell connections restore spatial-pattern vision in a person.
completion.criterion: In a person with optic-nerve damage, regenerated retinal ganglion cell axons reconnect the retina to brain visual targets, transmit spatially ordered signals, and restore discrimination of spatial patterns. Anatomical and physiological evidence attributes the recovered function to the new connections rather than improved function of surviving pathways.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; provisional synthesis of NEI connectivity goals and the RReSTORe Consortium’s mapping goal.
completion.basis: Searches of NEI AGI reports, RReSTORe, ARPA-H THEA, FDA pages and ClinicalTrials.gov found no published human success criterion combining new axons, retinotopy and restored form vision. This provisional test combines the published connectivity and mapping goals with AGI’s distinction between regeneration and rescue of surviving neurons. No opened human result establishes that combination.

milestones.title: Retinal ganglion cell axons grow across an optic-nerve injury site in a mammal.
milestones.criterion: Axons extend beyond an optic-nerve injury site, establishing the proximal-growth stage identified by the NEI workshop. Lu and colleagues reported mouse RGC axons extending more than 5 mm into the optic chiasm after 12–16 weeks of Oct4, Sox2 and Klf4 expression; imaging at 16 weeks included two optic nerves. This establishes axon extension, without establishing retinotopic brain reconnection.
milestones.set_by: NEI AGI optic-nerve workshop, April 2015 report, section “Axon growth”.
milestones.threshold_quote: Proximal growth deals largely with the growth across an injury site

milestones.title: Regenerated retinal ganglion cell axons establish a retinotopic map in mammalian brain targets.
milestones.criterion: Regenerated RGC axons synapse at subcortical visual centres and establish a retinotopic map. The consortium specifies no numerical mapping-error tolerance. Lim and colleagues found regenerated, labelled RGC axons in appropriate visual nuclei in six of nine mice after three weeks of treatment; that result demonstrated target selection without establishing a within-target retinotopic map.
milestones.set_by: RReSTORe Consortium, 2023 roadmap, Table 5, “Retinotopic mapping” row. The published goal concerns RGC replacement; it also describes the required mapping outcome for endogenous regeneration. The test is stated in a table.

milestones.title: A treatment produces optic-nerve axon regeneration in a nonhuman primate.
milestones.criterion: An intervention extends optic-nerve regeneration to a nonhuman-primate model, the translational step identified by the NEI workshop. Its report specifies no minimum axon count, regeneration distance or visual-acuity gain. Preservation of existing neurons or retinal engraftment alone does not demonstrate regenerated eye-to-brain connections.
milestones.set_by: NEI AGI optic-nerve workshop, April 2015 report, section “Animal Models: Species Selection”.
milestones.threshold_quote: the best candidate therapies should be tested in primates

milestones.title: A retinal ganglion cell repair treatment causes no detrimental visual effect in initial human testing.
milestones.criterion: Initial human testing finds no detrimental effect on visual function after treatment, with follow-up defined by the study protocol. AGI prescribes no common sample size or observation period. On 8 October 2026, Life Biosciences reported no dose-limiting toxicities or serious adverse events through day 56 in three ER-100 recipients with open-angle glaucoma. These interim safety observations were not peer reviewed and did not establish reconnection.
milestones.set_by: NEI AGI clinical-development town-hall report, 2017, section “Assessing Safety and Efficacy”; written for retinal cell replacement.

milestones.title: Retinal ganglion cell repair improves visual function significantly in a controlled human study.
milestones.criterion: A human study demonstrates a statistically significant treatment-related improvement in visual function against a control comparison, using its prespecified analysis. The AGI report identifies statistical significance as the early proof-of-principle bar, without prescribing a universal effect size or significance level. This establishes functional benefit before establishing that new, retinotopically organised connections caused it.
milestones.set_by: NEI AGI clinical-development town-hall report, 2017, sections on control comparisons, functional endpoints and regulatory development; written for retinal cell replacement.
milestones.threshold_quote: a statistically significant difference needed for proof of principle.

not_found: No numerical human retinotopic mapping tolerance or reconnection-specific durability requirement was found.
No primary result establishing regenerated retinotopic eye-to-brain connections in a nonhuman primate was found.
No controlled human RGC-repair result meeting the stated functional proof-of-principle criterion was found.
The full text of the 2023 Med translational roadmap could not be opened at PMC or the publisher.
Readable full texts for the supplied citations 10.1016/j.tips.2024.11.008 and 10.1126/scitranslmed.adr1062 could not be opened.
